Topic: If you pass a child abandoned by the roadside, weeping in the autumn wind, and leave only a few coins and a poem before walking on toward your art, have you honored the sorrow of the world or merely used it?
Montaigne — Judgement:
I have always distrusted the man who feels most exquisitely when he has an audience, even if that audience is only his own future page. The question is whether the traveller's tears were for the child or for the verse the child would furnish.

I wrote that cowardice is the mother of cruelty, but I might have added that refinement is its aunt: we grow so skilled at contemplating suffering that we forget it has a body, which is cold and hungry now. I, who confessed to weeping easily at the miseries of others and could not watch a chicken's neck wrung without distress, know how cheaply pity is bought when it costs only sentiment. A poem keeps the child's sorrow alive for centuries; it does not keep the child alive until morning.

He who walks on has used the child, and his coins are the fee he paid for the material.

*Pity that keeps walking is only curiosity with a wet face.*
Nietzsche — Judgement:
You ask whether the poet who tosses coins and a verse to a weeping child has served sorrow or fed upon it; I ask what kind of will speaks through that gesture.

Pity, I have long warned, multiplies suffering and flatters the one who pities; yet this wanderer does not even pity honestly. He gives enough to quiet his conscience, takes the image for his poem, and calls the transaction reverence. The strong man either lifts the child with his own hands, out of overflowing power, or passes by with the hard honesty of one who knows his task lies elsewhere. This man does neither: he converts a living creature into an aesthetic ornament while pretending to have paid for it.

He has used the sorrow of the world, and worse, he has lied to himself about the using.

*He who leaves a coin and a poem beside suffering has purchased his own innocence cheaply, and the price was the child.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement:
A child left weeping by the road is no subject for verse but a claim upon the living, and I measure the passer-by not by the tenderness of his feeling but by what he owed and withheld.

In *Agrarian Justice* I argued that relief of the destitute is "not charity but a right" — a debt society owes to those it has dispossessed. The coins are a paltry instalment on that debt; the poem is a receipt the traveller writes to himself. To convert a child's abandonment into a fine melancholy is to do as Burke did with the French queen: pity the plumage and forget the dying bird.

He has used the sorrow of the world, and paid a few coppers for the privilege.

*Compassion that walks on has only purchased its subject cheaply.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
You ask whether the poet who tosses coins to a foundling and walks on has honoured grief or harvested it; I ask what moved him, for I hold that no man gives but with intention of good to himself.

Pity is nothing but the imagination of future calamity to ourselves, proceeding from the sense of another man's. The coins relieved the poet's own disquiet at the sight; the poem purchased him reputation, which is power. The child, meanwhile, remains in the very condition I described as the state of nature — solitary, poor, without a protector — and no verse ever stood guard over the weak, since covenants and compassions alike, without the sword, are but words.

He used the sorrow, and he used it cheaply, paying a few coins for a subject worth a lifetime of fame.

*He that relieves his own pity and leaves the sufferer in peril has bought himself ease, and called the purchase charity.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
I see in this roadside scene the old vice of sensibility: the traveller who weeps exquisitely over misery and mistakes his own tears for a discharge of duty.

I have long distrusted the cultivated feeling that makes of suffering an occasion for fine sentiment, as Burke mourned the plumage and forgot the dying bird. A child is not an emblem of autumn; it is a rational creature in embryo, with a claim of right upon every person able to preserve it. Coins and verses are alms, and alms flatter the giver while leaving the wretch exactly where he lay; it is justice, not charity, that is wanting in the world.

The poet who walks on has used the child's sorrow as material and abandoned the child a second time.

*Pity that does not stoop to lift is only vanity admiring its own tears.*
Hume — Judgement:
I take the case to be a trial of sympathy: whether a passion communicated by another's misery has moved the will, or merely furnished the imagination with an agreeable melancholy.

Reason alone never carries a man to a weeping child, nor away from one; only sentiment does. The cry by the roadside enters us by sympathy, that contagion which converts an idea of suffering into a lively impression. But a sentiment that ends in verse and a few coins has been enjoyed, not obeyed. I have observed that spectators love tragedy precisely because eloquence turns pain to pleasure, and the poet here has made himself a spectator of a real distress he had the power to relieve. Benevolence earns our approbation by its utility to the afflicted, and this child is no warmer for being well described.

He has used the sorrow of the world, and the coins are the fee he paid for it.

*Pity that stops at the poem is only taste wearing the mask of virtue.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
I take this to be the old question of the traveller-poet, and I put it thus: when we meet distress upon the road, is fellow-feeling discharged by the fineness of our emotion, or only by what we do for the sufferer?

In my *Theory of Moral Sentiments* I observed that a man would lose more sleep over his own little finger than over the ruin of a distant multitude; but this child is not distant. He lies within arm's reach, where nature has fitted our sympathy to act and where beneficence is plainly in our power. The impartial spectator within the breast does not applaud exquisite sensibility; he asks whether the infant was fed, warmed, and carried to a parish door. A poem makes the passer-by the object of admiration, and the child merely its occasion.

You have used the sorrow of the world, not honoured it.

*He who weeps beautifully over a misery he could have relieved has purchased his own praise with another's suffering.*
